Main.sentence: The National Security Agency ( NSA ) is an ___E:intelligence agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intelligence_agency)___ of the ___E:United States Department of Defense U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense)___ , under the authority of the ___E:director of national intelligence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_National_Intelligence)___ (DNI).

The NSA is responsible for global monitoring, collection, and processing of information and data for global intelligence and ___E:counterintelligence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Counterintelligence)___ purposes, specializing in a discipline known as ___E:signals intelligence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signals_intelligence)___ (SIGINT).

The NSA is also tasked with the ___E:protection U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_assurance)___ of U.S. communications networks and ___E:information systems U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Information_systems)___ .
The NSA relies on a variety of measures to accomplish its mission, the majority of which are ___E:clandestine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clandestine_operations)___ .
The NSA has roughly 32,000 employees.

Originating as a unit to decipher coded communications in ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ , it was officially formed as the NSA by President ___E:Harry S. Truman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman)___ in 1952. Between then and the end of the Cold War, it became the largest of the ___E:U.S. intelligence organizations U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._intelligence_community#Organization)___ in terms of personnel and budget.

Still, information available as of 2013 indicates that the ___E:Central Intelligence Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency)___ (CIA) pulled ahead in this regard, with a budget of $14.7 billion.

The NSA currently conducts ___E:worldwide mass data collection U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_surveillance)___ and has been known to physically ___E:bug U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bugging)___ electronic systems as one method to this end.  The NSA is also alleged to have been behind such attack software as ___E:Stuxnet U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stuxnet)___ , which severely damaged ___E:Iran's nuclear program U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuclear_program_of_Iran)___ .

The NSA, alongside the CIA, maintains a physical presence in many countries across the globe; the CIA/NSA joint ___E:Special Collection Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special_Collection_Service)___ (a highly classified intelligence team) inserts eavesdropping devices in high-value targets (such as presidential palaces or embassies).
SCS collection tactics allegedly encompass "close surveillance, burglary, wiretapping, [and] breaking".

Unlike the CIA and the ___E:Defense Intelligence Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Intelligence_Agency)___ (DIA), both of which specialize primarily in foreign ___E:human espionage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clandestine_human_intelligence)___ , the NSA does not publicly conduct ___E:human intelligence gathering U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_intelligence_(intelligence_gathering))___ .

The NSA is entrusted with assisting with and coordinating, SIGINT elements for other government organizations—which Executive Order prevents from engaging in such activities on their own.  As part of these responsibilities, the agency has a co-located organization called the ___E:Central Security Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Security_Service)___ (CSS), which facilitates cooperation between the NSA and other U.S. defense ___E:cryptanalysis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptanalysis)___ components.

To further ensure streamlined communication between the signals ___E:intelligence community U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Intelligence_Community)___ divisions, the ___E:NSA director U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Director_of_the_National_Security_Agency)___ simultaneously serves as the Commander of the ___E:United States Cyber Command U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Cyber_Command)___ and as Chief of the Central Security Service.

The NSA's actions have been a matter of political controversy on several occasions, including its role in providing intelligence during the ___E:Gulf of Tonkin incident U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Tonkin_incident)___ , which contributed to the ___E:escalation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Tonkin_Resolution)___ of U.S. involvement in the ___E:Vietnam War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War)___ .

Declassified documents later revealed that the NSA misinterpreted or overstated signals intelligence, leading to reports of a second ___E:North Vietnamese U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vietnam)___ attack that likely never occurred.

The agency has also received scrutiny for ___E:spying on anti–Vietnam War leaders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org#Vietnam_War)___ and the agency's participation in ___E:economic espionage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Economic_espionage)___ .

In 2013, the NSA had many of its secret surveillance programs ___E:revealed to the public U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Global_surveillance_disclosures_(2013%E2%80%93present))___ by ___E:Edward Snowden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden)___ , a former NSA contractor.
According to the leaked documents, the NSA intercepts and stores the communications of over a billion people worldwide, including United States citizens.
The documents also revealed that the NSA tracks hundreds of millions of people's movements using cell phone ___E:metadata U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metadata)___ .

Internationally, research has pointed to the NSA's ability to surveil the domestic Internet traffic of foreign countries through " ___E:boomerang routing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Network_Sovereignty#Protection_of_National_Traffic)___ ".

The origins of the National Security Agency can be traced back to April 28, 1917, three weeks after the ___E:U.S. Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Congress)___ declared war on Germany in ___E:World War I U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_I)___ .

A ___E:code U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_(cryptography))___ and ___E:cipher U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cipher)___ decryption unit was established as the Cable and Telegraph Section, which was also known as the Cipher Bureau.
It was headquartered in Washington, D.C., and was part of the war effort under the executive branch without direct congressional authorization.
During the war, it was relocated in the army's organizational chart several times.

On July 5, 1917, ___E:Herbert O. Yardley U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbert_O._Yardley)___ was assigned to head the unit. At that point, the unit consisted of Yardley and two ___E:civilian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civilian)___ clerks.

It absorbed the Navy's ___E:cryptanalysis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptanalysis)___ functions in July 1918. World War I ended on ___E:November 11, 1918 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Armistice_of_11_November_1918)___ , and the army cryptographic section of Military Intelligence (MI-8) moved to New York City on May 20, 1919, where it continued intelligence activities as the Code Compilation Company under the direction of Yardley.

After the disbandment of the ___E:U.S. Army U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army)___ cryptographic section of military intelligence known as MI-8, the U.S. government created the Cipher Bureau, also known as ___E:Black Chamber U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Chamber)___ , in 1919. The Black Chamber was the United States' first peacetime ___E:cryptanalytic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptanalytic)___ organization.

Jointly funded by the Army and the State Department, the Cipher Bureau was disguised as a ___E:New York City U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City)___ ___E:commercial code U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commercial_code_(communications))___ company; it produced and sold such codes for business use. Its true mission, however, was to break the communications (chiefly diplomatic) of other nations.

At the ___E:Washington Naval Conference U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Washington_Naval_Conference)___ , it aided American negotiators by providing them with the decrypted traffic of many of the conference delegations, including the ___E:Japanese U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Empire_of_Japan)___ .

The Black Chamber successfully persuaded ___E:Western Union U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Union)___ , the largest U.S. ___E:telegram U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Telegraphy)___ company at the time, as well as several other communications companies, to illegally give the Black Chamber access to cable traffic of foreign embassies and consulates.
Soon, these companies publicly discontinued their collaboration.
Despite the Chamber's initial successes, it was shut down in 1929 by U.S.
Secretary of State ___E:Henry L. Stimson U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_L._Stimson)___ , who defended his decision by stating, "Gentlemen do not read each other's mail."

During ___E:World War II U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_War_II)___ , the ___E:Signal Intelligence Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Signal_Intelligence_Service)___ (SIS) was created to intercept and decipher the communications of the ___E:Axis powers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Axis_powers)___ .

When the war ended, the SIS was reorganized as the ___E:Army Security Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Army_Security_Agency)___ (ASA), and it was placed under the leadership of the Director of Military Intelligence.
On May 20, 1949, all cryptologic activities were centralized under a national organization called the Armed Forces Security Agency (AFSA).

This organization was originally established within the ___E:U.S. Department of Defense U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_Defense)___ under the command of the ___E:Joint Chiefs of Staff U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joint_Chiefs_of_Staff)___ .

The AFSA was tasked with directing the Department of Defense communications and electronic intelligence activities, except those of U.S. ___E:military intelligence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Military_intelligence)___ units.

However, the AFSA was unable to centralize ___E:communications intelligence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COMINT)___ and failed to coordinate with civilian agencies that shared its interests, such as the ___E:Department of State U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Department_of_State)___ , the ___E:Central Intelligence Agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Intelligence_Agency)___ (CIA) and the ___E:Federal Bureau of Investigation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_Bureau_of_Investigation)___ (FBI).
In December 1951, President ___E:Harry S. Truman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harry_S._Truman)___ ordered a panel to investigate how AFSA had failed to achieve its goals.
The results of the investigation led to improvements and its redesignation as the National Security Agency.

The ___E:National Security Council U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_National_Security_Council)___ issued a memorandum of October 24, 1952, that revised ___E:National Security Council Intelligence Directive (NSCID) 9 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Council_Intelligence_Directives)___ .

On the same day, Truman issued a second memorandum that called for the establishment of the NSA.  The actual establishment of the NSA was done by a November 4 memo by ___E:Robert A. Lovett U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_A._Lovett)___ , the ___E:Secretary of Defense U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Secretary_of_Defense)___ , changing the name of the AFSA to the NSA, and making the new agency responsible for all communications intelligence.

Since President Truman's memo was a ___E:classified U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Classified_information)___ document,  the existence of the NSA was not known to the public at that time. Due to its ultra-secrecy, the U.S. intelligence community referred to the NSA as "No Such Agency".

In the 1960s, the NSA played a key role in expanding American commitment to the ___E:Vietnam War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War)___ by providing evidence of a ___E:North Vietnamese U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Vietnam)___ attack on the American Naval destroyer ___E:USS Maddox U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/USS_Maddox_(DD-731))___ during the ___E:Gulf of Tonkin incident U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gulf_of_Tonkin_incident)___ .

A secret operation, code-named " ___E:MINARET U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Project_MINARET)___ ", was set up by the NSA to monitor the phone communications of Senators ___E:Frank Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Church)___ and ___E:Howard Baker U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Howard_Baker)___ , as well as key leaders of the ___E:civil rights movement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civil_rights_movement)___ , including ___E:Martin Luther King Jr. U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Martin_Luther_King_Jr.)___ , and prominent U.S. journalists and athletes who criticized the ___E:Vietnam War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War)___ .
However, the project turned out to be controversial, and an internal review by the NSA concluded that its Minaret program was "disreputable if not outright illegal".
The NSA has mounted a major effort to secure tactical communications among U.S. armed forces during the war with mixed success.

The ___E:NESTOR U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NESTOR_(encryption))___ family of compatible ___E:secure voice U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Secure_voice)___ systems it developed was widely deployed during the ___E:Vietnam War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vietnam_War)___ , with about 30,000 NESTOR sets produced.
However, a variety of technical and operational problems limited their use, allowing the North Vietnamese to exploit and intercept U.S. communications.  : Vol I, p.79

In the aftermath of the ___E:Watergate scandal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Watergate_scandal)___ , a congressional hearing in 1975 led by Senator ___E:Frank Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Church)___  revealed that the NSA, in collaboration with Britain's SIGINT intelligence agency, ___E:Government Communications Headquarters U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Communications_Headquarters)___ (GCHQ), had routinely intercepted the international communications of prominent anti-Vietnam war leaders such as ___E:Jane Fonda U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jane_Fonda)___ and Dr. ___E:Benjamin Spock U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Spock)___ .

The NSA tracked these individuals in a secret filing system that was destroyed in 1974.  Following the resignation of President ___E:Richard Nixon U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Nixon)___ , there were several investigations into suspected misuse of FBI, CIA and NSA facilities.

Senator ___E:Frank Church U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frank_Church)___ uncovered previously unknown activity,  such as a CIA plot (ordered by the administration of President ___E:John F. Kennedy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_F._Kennedy)___ ) to assassinate ___E:Fidel Castro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fidel_Castro)___ .
The investigation also uncovered NSA's wiretaps on targeted U.S. citizens.
After the Church Committee hearings, the ___E:Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Intelligence_Surveillance_Act)___ of 1978 was passed.
This was designed to limit the practice of ___E:mass surveillance in the United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mass_surveillance_in_the_United_States)___ .

In 1986, the NSA intercepted the communications of the Libyan government during the immediate aftermath of the ___E:Berlin discotheque bombing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_Berlin_discotheque_bombing)___ .
The ___E:White House U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_House)___ asserted that the NSA interception had provided "irrefutable" evidence that Libya was behind the bombing, which U.S.

President ___E:Ronald Reagan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ronald_Reagan)___ cited as a justification for the ___E:1986 United States bombing of Libya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1986_United_States_bombing_of_Libya)___ .

In 1999, a multi-year investigation by the European Parliament highlighted the NSA's role in economic espionage in a report entitled 'Development of Surveillance Technology and Risk of Abuse of Economic Information'.

That year, the NSA founded the ___E:NSA Hall of Honor U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NSA_Hall_of_Honor)___ , a memorial at the ___E:National Cryptologic Museum U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Cryptologic_Museum)___ in Fort Meade, Maryland.
The memorial is a, "tribute to the pioneers and heroes who have made significant and long-lasting contributions to American cryptology".
NSA employees must be retired for more than fifteen years to qualify for the memorial.
NSA's infrastructure deteriorated in the 1990s as defense budget cuts resulted in maintenance deferrals.
On January 24, 2000, NSA headquarters suffered a total network outage for three days caused by an overloaded network.
Incoming traffic was successfully stored on agency servers, but it could not be directed and processed.

The agency carried out emergency repairs for $3 million to get the system running again (some incoming traffic was also directed instead to Britain's ___E:GCHQ U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/GCHQ)___ for the time being).
Director ___E:Michael Hayden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michael_Hayden_(general))___ called the outage a "wake-up call" for the need to invest in the agency's infrastructure.

In the 1990s the defensive arm of the NSA—the Information Assurance Directorate (IAD)—started working more openly; the first public technical talk by an NSA scientist at a major cryptography conference was J. Solinas' presentation on efficient ___E:Elliptic Curve Cryptography U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elliptic-curve_cryptography)___ algorithms at Crypto 1997.  The IAD's cooperative approach to academia and industry culminated in its support for a ___E:transparent process U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Encryption_Standard_process)___ for replacing the outdated ___E:Data Encryption Standard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_Encryption_Standard)___ (DES) by an ___E:Advanced Encryption Standard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_Encryption_Standard)___ (AES).

Cybersecurity policy expert ___E:Susan Landau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Landau)___ attributes the NSA's harmonious collaboration with industry and academia in the selection of the AES in 2000—and the Agency's support for the choice of a strong encryption algorithm designed by Europeans rather than by Americans—to ___E:Brian Snow U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brian_Snow)___ , who was the Technical Director of IAD and represented the NSA as cochairman of the Technical Working Group for the AES competition, and Michael Jacobs, who headed IAD at the time.  : 75

After the ___E:terrorist attacks of September 11, 2001 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ , the NSA believed that it had public support for a dramatic expansion of its surveillance activities.

According to ___E:Neal Koblitz U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neal_Koblitz)___ and ___E:Alfred Menezes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alfred_Menezes)___ , the period when the NSA was a trusted partner with academia and industry in the development of cryptographic standards started to come to an end when, as part of the change in the NSA in the post-September 11 era, Snow was replaced as Technical Director, Jacobs retired, and IAD could no longer effectively oppose proposed actions by the offensive arm of the NSA.

In the aftermath of the ___E:September 11 attacks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/September_11_attacks)___ , the NSA created new IT systems to deal with the flood of information from new technologies like the Internet and cell phones. ___E:ThinThread U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ThinThread)___ contained advanced ___E:data mining U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_mining)___ capabilities.
It also had a "privacy mechanism"; surveillance was stored encrypted; decryption required a warrant.
The research done under this program may have contributed to the technology used in later systems.
ThinThread was canceled when Michael Hayden chose ___E:Trailblazer U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trailblazer_Project)___ , which did not include ThinThread's privacy system.

___E:Trailblazer Project U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trailblazer_Project)___ ramped up in 2002 and was worked on by ___E:Science Applications International Corporation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_Applications_International_Corporation)___ (SAIC), ___E:Boeing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boeing)___ , ___E:Computer Sciences Corporation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_Sciences_Corporation)___ , ___E:IBM U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IBM)___ , and ___E:Litton Industries U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Litton_Industries)___ .
Some NSA ___E:whistleblowers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whistleblower)___ complained internally about major problems surrounding Trailblazer.
This led to investigations by Congress and the NSA and DoD ___E:Inspectors General U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inspectors_General)___ .

The project was canceled in early 2004. ___E:Turbulence U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turbulence_(NSA))___ started in 2005. It was developed in small, inexpensive "test" pieces, rather than one grand plan like Trailblazer.
It also included offensive cyber-warfare capabilities, like injecting ___E:malware U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malware)___ into remote computers.
Congress criticized Turbulence in 2007 for having similar bureaucratic problems as Trailblazer.
It was to be a realization of information processing at higher speeds in cyberspace.

The massive extent of the NSA's spying, both foreign and domestic, was revealed to the public in a series of detailed disclosures of internal NSA documents beginning in June 2013. Most of the disclosures were leaked by former NSA contractor ___E:Edward Snowden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden)___ .
On 4 September 2020, the NSA's surveillance program was ruled unlawful by the ___E:US Court of Appeals U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Courts_of_Appeals)___ .
The court also added that the US intelligence leaders, who publicly defended it, were not telling the truth.

NSA's ___E:eavesdropping U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eavesdropping)___ mission includes radio broadcasting, both from various organizations and individuals, the Internet, telephone calls, and other intercepted forms of communication.
Its secure communications mission includes military, diplomatic, and all other sensitive, confidential, or secret government communications.

According to a 2010 article in The Washington Post , "every day, collection systems at the National Security Agency intercept and store 1.7 billion e-mails, phone calls and other types of communications.
The NSA sorts a fraction of those into 70 separate databases."

Because of its listening task, NSA/CSS has been heavily involved in ___E:cryptanalytic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cryptanalysis)___ research, continuing the work of predecessor agencies which had broken many World War II ___E:codes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_(cryptography))___ and ___E:ciphers U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cipher)___ (see, for instance, ___E:Purple U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_(cipher_machine))___ , ___E:Venona project U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venona_project)___ , and ___E:JN-25 U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/JN-25)___ ).

In 2004, NSA ___E:Central Security Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Central_Security_Service)___ and the ___E:National Cyber Security Division U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Cyber_Security_Division)___ of the ___E:Department of Homeland Security U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Homeland_Security)___ (DHS) agreed to expand the NSA Centers of Academic Excellence in Information Assurance Education Program.

As part of the ___E:National Security Presidential Directive U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Security_Directive)___ 54/Homeland Security Presidential Directive 23 (NSPD 54), signed on January 8, 2008, by President Bush, the NSA became the lead agency to monitor and protect all of the federal government's computer networks from ___E:cyber-terrorism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyber-terrorism)___ .
A part of the NSA's mission is to serve as a ___E:combat support agency U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Combat_support_agency)___ for the Department of Defense.
Operations by the National Security Agency can be divided into three types:
"Echelon" was created in the incubator of the ___E:Cold War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cold_War)___ .
Today it is a ___E:legacy system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Legacy_system)___ , and several NSA stations are closing.

NSA/CSS, in combination with the equivalent agencies in the United Kingdom ( ___E:Government Communications Headquarters U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Communications_Headquarters)___ ), Canada ( ___E:Communications Security Establishment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Communications_Security_Establishment)___ ), Australia ( ___E:Australian Signals Directorate U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australian_Signals_Directorate)___ ), and New Zealand ( ___E:Government Communications Security Bureau U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_Communications_Security_Bureau)___ ), otherwise known as the ___E:UKUSA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UKUSA_Agreement)___ group,  was reported to be in command of the operation of the so-called ___E:ECHELON U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECHELON)___ system.
Its capabilities were suspected to include the ability to monitor a large proportion of the world's transmitted civilian telephone, fax, and data traffic.

During the early 1970s, the first of what became more than eight large satellite communications dishes were installed at Menwith Hill.  Investigative journalist ___E:Duncan Campbell U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duncan_Campbell_(journalist,_born_1952))___ reported in 1988 on the " ___E:ECHELON U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ECHELON)___ " surveillance program, an extension of the ___E:UKUSA Agreement U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UKUSA_Agreement)___ on global signals intelligence ___E:SIGINT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SIGINT)___ , and detailed how the eavesdropping operations worked.

On November 3, 1999, the BBC reported that they had confirmation from the Australian Government of the existence of a powerful "global spying network" code-named Echelon, that could "eavesdrop on every single phone call, fax or e-mail, anywhere on the planet" with Britain and the United States as the chief protagonists.
They confirmed that Menwith Hill was "linked directly to the headquarters of the US National Security Agency (NSA) at Fort Meade in Maryland".

NSA's United States Signals Intelligence Directive 18 (USSID 18) strictly prohibited the interception or collection of information about "... ___E:U.S. persons U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._person)___ , entities, corporations or organizations...." without explicit written legal permission from the ___E:United States Attorney General U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Attorney_General)___ when the subject is located abroad, or the ___E:Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_Intelligence_Surveillance_Court)___ when within U.S. borders.

Alleged Echelon-related activities, including its use for motives other than national security, including political and ___E:industrial espionage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Industrial_espionage)___ , received criticism from countries outside the UKUSA alliance.

The NSA was also involved in planning to blackmail people with " ___E:SEXINT U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SEXINT)___ ", intelligence gained about a potential target's sexual activity and preferences.

Those targeted had not committed any apparent crime nor were they charged with one.  To support its ___E:facial recognition U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Facial_recognition_system)___ program, the NSA is intercepting "millions of images per day".

The ___E:Real Time Regional Gateway U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Real_Time_Regional_Gateway)___ is a data collection program introduced in 2005 in Iraq by the NSA during the ___E:Iraq War U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iraq_War)___ that consisted of gathering all electronic communication, storing it, then searching and otherwise analyzing it. It was effective in providing information about Iraqi insurgents who had eluded less comprehensive techniques.

This "collect it all" strategy introduced by NSA director, ___E:Keith B. Alexander U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_B._Alexander)___ , is believed by ___E:Glenn Greenwald U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glenn_Greenwald)___ of The Guardian to be the model for the comprehensive worldwide mass archiving of communications which NSA is engaged in as of 2013.

A dedicated unit of the NSA locates targets for the ___E:CIA U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/CIA)___ for extrajudicial assassination in the Middle East.  The NSA has also spied extensively on the European Union, the United Nations, and numerous governments including allies and trading partners in Europe, South America, and Asia.   In June 2015, ___E:WikiLeaks U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WikiLeaks)___ published documents showing that NSA spied on ___E:French U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France)___ companies.
WikiLeaks also published documents showing that NSA spied on federal German ministries since the 1990s.
Even Germany's Chancellor ___E:Angela Merkel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angela_Merkel)___ 's cellphones and phones of her predecessors had been intercepted.

In June 2013, ___E:Edward Snowden U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edward_Snowden)___ revealed that between 8 February and 8 March 2013, the NSA collected about 124.8 billion telephone data items and 97.1 billion computer data items throughout the world, as was displayed in charts from an internal NSA tool codenamed ___E:Boundless Informant U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundless_Informant)___ .

Initially, it was reported that some of these data reflected eavesdropping on citizens in countries like Germany, Spain, and France,  but later on, it became clear that those data were collected by European agencies during military missions abroad and were subsequently shared with NSA.

The NSA conducts ___E:polygraph U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polygraph)___ tests of employees.
For new employees, the tests are meant to discover enemy spies who are applying to the NSA and to uncover any information that could make an applicant pliant to coercion.
As part of the latter, historically EPQs or "embarrassing personal questions" about sexual behavior had been included in the NSA polygraph.
The NSA also conducts five-year periodic reinvestigation polygraphs of employees, focusing on counterintelligence programs.

In addition, the NSA conducts periodic polygraph investigations to find spies and leakers; those who refuse to take them may receive "termination of employment", according to a 1982 memorandum from the director of the NSA.

There are also "special access examination" polygraphs for employees who wish to work in highly sensitive areas, and those polygraphs cover counterintelligence questions and some questions about behavior.
NSA's brochure states that the average test length is between two and four hours.

A 1983 report of the ___E:Office of Technology Assessment U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Office_of_Technology_Assessment)___ stated that "It appears that the NSA [National Security Agency] (and possibly CIA) use the polygraph not to determine deception or truthfulness per se, but as a technique of interrogation to encourage admissions."  Sometimes applicants in the polygraph process confess to committing felonies such as murder, rape, and selling of illegal drugs.
Between 1974 and 1979, of the 20,511 job applicants who took polygraph tests, 695 (3.4%) confessed to previous felony crimes; almost all of those crimes had been undetected.

The video, ten minutes long, is titled "The Truth About the Polygraph" and was posted to the Web site of the ___E:Defense Security Service U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defense_Security_Service)___ .

Jeff Stein of The Washington Post said that the video portrays "various applicants, or actors playing them—it's not clear—describing everything bad they had heard about the test, the implication being that none of it is true."  AntiPolygraph.org argues that the NSA-produced video omits some information about the polygraph process; it produced a video responding to the NSA video.
George Maschke, the founder of the Web site, accused the NSA polygraph video of being " ___E:Orwellian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orwellian)___ ".

Edward Snowden is a former American intelligence contractor who revealed in 2013 the existence of secret wide-ranging information-gathering programs conducted by the National Security Agency (NSA).

More specifically, Snowden released information that demonstrated how the United States government was gathering immense amounts of personal communications, emails, phone locations, web histories and more of American citizens without their knowledge.

One of Snowden's primary motivators for releasing this information was fear of a surveillance state developing as a result of the infrastructure being created by the NSA. As Snowden recounts, "I believe that, at this point in history, the greatest danger to our freedom and way of life comes from the reasonable fear of omniscient State powers kept in check by nothing more than policy documents...
It is not that I do not value intelligence, but that I oppose . . . omniscient, automatic, mass surveillance. . . .
That seems to me a greater threat to the institutions of free society than missed intelligence reports, and unworthy of the costs."
